Disclosure Questions P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 P7 P8 P9
6.  Performance of the 
entity against the specific 
commitments, goals and 
targets along with reasons in 
case the same are not met.Environment
Renewable Energy: The Company has continued to make progress toward its renewable 
energy transition goals. While the near term target of 30% renewable energy consumption by 
Financial Year 2024-25 has not been fully achieved, meaningful advancement has been made 
through on-site solar installations and energy efficiency initiatives across manufacturing 
facilities. The shortfall is attributable to the capital intensity of renewable infrastructure 
deployment and the pace of regulatory approvals for additional solar capacity. The Company 
remains firmly committed to its medium term target of 40% renewable energy by Financial 
Year 2027-28 and is actively evaluating Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and further  
on-site capacity expansion to accelerate progress.
Zero Waste to Landfill: The Company has established structured waste segregation, 
recovery, and recycling programmes across all manufacturing locations. High value metallic 
scrap and polymer waste are systematically channelled through certified recyclers and 
recovery partners. A comprehensive waste tracking baseline is being formalised in Financial  
Year 2025-26 to enable quantitative monitoring of progress toward this goal.
Social
Occupational Health and Safety: The Company conducted 336 safety rounds during Financial 
Year 2025-26, resulting in identification and full closure of 2,688 safety observations, with 
no open items remaining at year end. A structured framework of Behaviour Based Safety, 
Kaizen driven continuous improvement, and periodic audits continues to underpin our 
OHS management. During the Financial Year, 2 Lost Time Injuries and 2 High consequence  
incidents were regrettably recorded, and immediate corrective actions including installation 
of machine interlocks and redesign of safety guards were implemented at the affected 
locations. The Company remains committed to strengthening preventive controls to drive 
toward zero major incidents.
Diversity and Inclusion Female Representation: The Company continues to advance its 
gender diversity agenda across locations. As of Financial Year 2025 - 26, female representation 
across the combined workforce (employees and workers) stands at approximately 9%. On the 
workers’ category specifically, the Company has achieved a female representation of 32%, 
surpassing the stated target of 25% by March 2025. The target of 12% female representation 
among employees remains under active pursuit, with targeted recruitment drives ongoing 
across locations. Category wise disaggregated data is being further strengthened to enable 
consistent and precise tracking against each sub target going forward. With respect to 
Persons with Disabilities (PwD), structured inclusion pilots have been initiated at Rajpura and 
Power-One, and a roadmap for tracking year-on-year PwD hiring trends is being developed.
Persons with Disabilities: The Company continues to embed inclusive hiring practices within 
its recruitment framework. As of Financial Year 2025 - 26, the total number of differently 
abled employees and workers stands at 33, reflecting a marginal year-on-year increase over 
32 in Financial Year 2024 - 25. While the Company has achieved the stated objective of 
a year-on-year increase, it acknowledges that progress remains modest and is committed 
to strengthening its inclusive hiring initiatives to meaningfully improve representation of 
persons with disabilities across its workforce in the coming years.
Governance
Research and Development: The Company has materially strengthened its R&D investment 
in Financial Year 2025 - 26, with a total spend of approximately ` 80 Crore, encompassing 
development infrastructure, tooling, and testing capabilities. A total of approximately 111 
models were developed during the Financial Year spanning new platform creation, design 
enhancement, and customer-specific programmes. A landmark achievement during the 
Financial Year was the establishment of India’s third 30 ton psychrometric testing laboratory, 
significantly expanding our product development capability. Cost innovation of ` 7.25 Crore 
was realised through BOM rationalisation and process optimisation. These outcomes reflect 
sustained and growing commitment to innovation led and sustainable growth, consistent 
with the stated governance goal.

10. Health and safety management system: 
a)  Whether an Occupational Health and Safety Management System has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/No). If yes, the 
coverage such system?
  Yes, the Company has implemented a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management system across all its 
offices and manufacturing facilities. 
  Coverage: The OHS management system covers the Company’s total workforce, including permanent employees, contractual 
workers, and on-site third party personnel across all facilities.
 Key elements of the system include:
  Dedicated EHS Teams: Each facility has a dedicated Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) team that works in coordination with 
site management and plant heads to conduct regular workplace inspections and hazard identification exercises.
  Safety Committees: A safety committee has been constituted at every facility to raise and escalate health and safety concerns 
to management. Issues are reviewed and resolved through monthly management review meetings.
  Audits: Periodic safety and environment audits are conducted at all plants through external agencies to assess compliance, 
identify gaps, and drive continuous improvement in safety standards.
b)  What are the processes used to identify work related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non routine basis by the 
entity? 
  The Company uses a structured approach to identify work related hazards and assess risks, covering both routine and  
non routine situations:
 Routine Processes:
 •  Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA): HIRA is conducted periodically across all facilities to systematically 
identify hazards, evaluate the likelihood and severity of potential impacts, and implement appropriate control measures. 
HIRA exercises are carried out by the EHS and site management teams.
 •  Periodic Internal Audits: Scheduled internal safety audits and workplace inspections are conducted to identify unsafe acts, 
unsafe conditions, and compliance gaps. Findings are documented and tracked to closure.
 •  Leadership Safety Rounds: Senior management and plant heads conduct regular safety walkthrough rounds to reinforce 
safety culture and identify on ground risks that may not surface through formal audits.
 Non-Routine Processes:
 •  Incident Investigation and CAPA: When an incident, near-miss, or unsafe condition is reported, a root cause analysis 
is conducted and Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA) are identified and implemented. The EHS team monitors 
implementation and, where required, re evaluates the effectiveness of the actions taken.
  Follow-up on all identified actions both routine and non routine is undertaken by the EHS and site management teams to ensure 
timely closure and sustained effectiveness.
=== page 221 ===
218
Annual Report 2025-26
c)  Whether you have processes for workers to report the work related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. 
(Y/N)
  Yes. The Company has established processes enabling workers to report work-related hazards and, where necessary, remove 
themselves from situations of serious or imminent risk.
  Hazard Reporting: All employees and workers are encouraged and empowered to report unsafe acts, unsafe conditions, or 
work related hazards through the following channels:
 • Reporting to the site EHS team or immediate supervisor
 • Escalation to the facility Safety Committee
  All reported hazards are logged, investigated, and tracked to closure. The Safety Committee reviews reported concerns during 
monthly management review meetings to ensure timely resolution.
  Right to Remove from Risk: Workers have the right to remove themselves from work situations that they reasonably believe 
present serious or imminent danger to their life or health, without fear of reprisal or disciplinary action. The Company ensures 
that no worker is penalised for exercising this right in good faith.
d)  Do the employees/worker of the entity have access to non occupational medical and healthcare services? (Yes/No) 
  Yes. The Company provides access to non occupational medical and healthcare services to its employees and workers. The 
following healthcare support is made available:
 •  Group Mediclaim Insurance: Permanent employees and workers are covered under a group Mediclaim policy, providing 
financial protection against hospitalisation and medical expenses.
 •  Annual Health Check ups: The Company conducts periodic health check ups for employees at all facilities, covering 
general physical examinations, blood tests, and other relevant diagnostics, in coordination with empanelled medical 
professionals.
 •  Wellness Initiatives: The Company promotes employee well being through health awareness sessions, fitness activities, 
and periodic health drives such as eye camps and blood donation drives.

12. Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy workplace. 
  The Company places significant emphasis on occupational health and safety and is committed to maintaining the highest 
standards while complying with all applicable environment, health, and safety laws.
  Monitoring and Audits: EHS and site management teams conduct regular gemba walks, monthly audits, workplace inspections, 
and hazard identification exercises. Senior management and the central HR team undertake surprise facility visits to assess 
ground level conditions. Factory wide safety and environmental audits are also conducted by competent authorities to ensure 
compliance with the Factories Act.
  Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): All employees and workers are provided with job appropriate PPE, including gloves, 
helmets, and eye and ear protection, to safeguard against workplace hazards.
  Training and Awareness: Regular health and safety training sessions are conducted covering work related hazards, safe 
operation of machinery, emergency procedures, fire safety, and first aid.
  Emergency Preparedness: A Safety Committee and Emergency Response Team (ERT) comprising first responders and 
firefighters  are established at all plants. Quarterly mock drills are conducted across all facilities, and an annual Safety Week is 
observed.
  Workplace Monitoring and Signage: Workplace and work zone monitoring is carried out at all facilities. Safety signs, general 
safety instructions in local languages, and life safety rules are prominently displayed across all workstations.

Annual Report 2025-2615.  Provide details of any corrective action taken or underway to address safety related incidents (if any) and on significant 
risks/concerns arising from assessments of health & safety practices and working conditions. 
  The Company has established a structured process to address safety related incidents and risks identified through health and 
safety assessments.
  Incident Response and Corrective Action: In the event of any safety incident or near miss, a root cause analysis is conducted 
by the EHS and site management teams. Based on the findings, Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA) are identified, 
implemented, and tracked to closure. Learnings from each incident including the root cause, corrective measures taken, and 
steps to prevent recurrence are shared across all facilities within the Amber Group to ensure systemic improvement and avoid 
future occurrences.
  Risks and Concerns from Assessments: Significant risks and concerns identified through routine HIRA exercises, internal audits, 
gemba walks, and external audits are logged and prioritised based on their severity. Action plans are developed to eliminate or 
mitigate these risks within defined timelines, with periodic follow up by the EHS team to assess effectiveness.
1.  Does the entity extend any life insurance or any compensatory package in the event of death of Employees and Workers
(A)  Employees - Yes. The Company provides the following insurance coverage to all permanent employees:
 i.  Group Personal Accident (GPA) Insurance: Covers death or disability arising from accidents.
 ii.  Group Medical Insurance (GMI): The Company provides Group Medical Insurance coverage to its employees, ensuring 
financial protection and access to quality healthcare services for them and their eligible dependents.
 iii.  Group Term Life Insurance (GTLI): Provides life cover to employees, ensuring financial support to their family in the event of 
death during the term of employment.
(B)  Workers - Yes. The Company provides Group Personal Accident (GPA) Insurance to all permanent workers, covering death or

  Due Diligence and Audits: Necessary due diligence is conducted while processing vendor invoices, and regular audits of value 
chain partners are carried out to assess compliance. As part of mandatory checks, the Company verifies that vendors make 
requisite deductions and contributions towards PF, ESI, and GST, in accordance with applicable statutory requirements.
  Timely Payments: The Company is committed to making timely payments to its employees, workers, and vendors in compliance 
with statutory obligations. This reflects the Company’s broader commitment to ethical and responsible business conduct across 
its value chain.

1. Describe the processes for identifying key stakeholder groups of the entity. 
  The Company identifies its key stakeholder groups through a structured stakeholder mapping process that considers the nature 
and extent of each group’s interaction with, and impact on, the Company’s business operations and value chain.
 Stakeholders are identified based on criteria such as:
 • Dependency: Groups that depend on the Company’s activities, products, or decisions
 • Influence: Groups that can significantly affect the Company’s ability to achieve its objectives
 • Responsibility: Groups towards whom the Company has legal, ethical, or contractual obligations
 • Impact: Groups affected positively or negatively by the Company’s operations
  Based on this assessment, the Company’s key stakeholder groups include permanent and contractual employees, suppliers and 
vendors, local communities, investors and shareholders, banks and financial institutions, and regulators.
  To ensure structured and meaningful engagement with these groups, the Company has formulated a Stakeholder Engagement 
Policy, which provides a formal framework for addressing stakeholder needs and concerns, rooted in the Company’s core values 
of transparency, accountability, and trust.

5. Describe the internal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.  
  The Company regards respect for human rights as a core value and is committed to ensuring fair, ethical and inclusive business 
and employment practices. The Company maintains a zero tolerance policy towards discrimination, harassment, forced labour, 
child labour, human trafficking and all forms of physical, sexual, psychological or verbal abuse.
 Grievance Redressal Mechanisms:
  The Company has established the following internal mechanisms to enable stakeholders to raise and resolve human rights 
related grievances:
 •  Open Door Policy: Employees are encouraged to raise concerns directly with senior management or the Human Resources 
team at any time, ensuring accessible and informal channels for early resolution.
 •  Complaint and Suggestion Boxes: Physical complaint/suggestion boxes are available at all facilities, providing an accessible 
and confidential channel for employees and workers to register concerns.
 •  Internal Complaints Committee (ICC): In accordance with the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, 
Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, (“PoSH Act”) an Internal Complaints Committee is constituted to receive, investigate, 
and resolve complaints related to sexual harassment at the workplace.
 •  Whistleblower/Vigil Mechanism: employees may report concerns regarding human rights violations, unethical conduct, or 
policy breaches through the Company’s vigil mechanism, which ensures confidentiality and protection against retaliation.
 •  Escalation and Resolution: Complaints received through any channel are reviewed by the HR team and escalated to senior 
management or the relevant committee as appropriate. Resolutions are communicated to the complainant and appropriate 
confidentiality maintained throughout the process.
  The Company’s Human Rights Policy, developed in alignment with internationally and nationally recognised human rights 
frameworks, underpins these mechanisms and reinforces the Company’s commitment to a safe and harmonious workplace.
 Policy available at: https:/ /www.ir.ambergroupindia.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/3.-Human-Rights-Policy.pdf

8. Mechanisms to prevent adverse consequences to the complainant in discrimination and harassment cases. 
  The Company is committed to maintaining a workplace free from violence, harassment, intimidation and all forms of 
discrimination. Every employee has the right to work in an environment that upholds their privacy, dignity, and safety.
  Whistleblower Policy: The Company has a formal Whistleblower (Vigil Mechanism) Policy that enables directors, employees 
and associates to report concerns regarding unethical behaviour, actual or suspected fraud or violations of Company policies. 
The policy explicitly mandates that the Vigilance Officer ensures appropriate safeguards against discrimination, victimisation, 
retaliation, demotion or any unfair employment practice against individuals who raise concerns in good faith.
  Prevention of Sexual Harassment (PoSH): The Company has a comprehensive Policy on Prevention of Sexual Harassment 
at the Workplace, framed in accordance with the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition, and 
Redressal) Act, 2013 (“PoSH Act”). An Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) has been constituted as required under the Act 
to receive, investigate and resolve complaints. The ICC process ensures strict confidentiality for all parties and prohibits 
retaliation against complainants at any stage of the proceedings.
  Awareness and Training: All employees are made aware of the grievance redressal mechanism, Whistleblower Policy and 
PoSH Policy through dedicated awareness sessions and policy communications. These policies are also covered as part of the 
employee induction programme for new hires, ensuring familiarity from the outset of employment.
9. Do human rights requirements form part of your business agreements and contracts?  (Yes/No)
  The Company does not currently incorporate explicit human rights clauses within its standard business agreements and 
contracts. However, the Company expects all value chain partners, vendors, and entities acting on its behalf to uphold human 
rights principles and operate within applicable legal and ethical frameworks.
  Human rights expectations are communicated to value chain partners through supplier onboarding processes, vendor 
codes of conduct, compliance declarations, or audit requirements. The Company prioritises partnerships with suppliers who 
demonstrate alignment with these principles and conducts due diligence to assess compliance during the partner evaluation 
process.
  The Company recognises the importance of formalising human rights requirements within its contractual framework and is 
evaluating explicit human rights provisions into its standard agreements as part of its broader commitment to responsible 
and ethical business conduct.

Annual Report 2025-265. Has the entity implemented a mechanism for Zero Liquid Discharge? If yes, provide details of its coverage and implementation. 
  Yes, the Company has implemented Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) mechanisms at select facilities, with efforts underway to expand 
coverage across its operations.
  ZLD Facilities: The Company’s Chennai, Supa and Ascent facilities operate as full Zero Liquid Discharge facilities, ensuring that 
no liquid waste is discharged from these sites. These facilities serve as models for sustainable water management within the 
Company’s operations.
  Minimal Liquid Discharge Facilities: The remaining facilities are equipped with internal wastewater treatment systems that 
operate on a minimal liquid discharge basis. Treated wastewater from these facilities is reused within operations including in the 
manufacturing process, landscaping, and flushing thereby significantly reducing freshwater consumption and minimising liquid 
discharge.
  Future Commitments: The Company is committed to progressively advancing towards minimal or zero liquid discharge across 
all its facilities and continues to evaluate opportunities to strengthen its water management practices.

manage such wastes. 
  The Company has implemented comprehensive waste management practices across all its facilities, with a focus on waste 
reduction, safe disposal, and minimising environmental impact.
 Waste Segregation and Storage:  
  A structured waste segregation system is in place across all facilities, categorising waste into hazardous and non-hazardous 
streams. Dedicated storage areas are allocated for specific waste categories including paper, plastic, e-waste, and hazardous 
waste ensuring organised and compliant management of each stream.
 Disposal and Recycling:
  Hazardous waste is disposed of through partnerships with the nearest Common Hazardous Waste Treatment, Storage and 
Disposal Facilities (CHWTSDF), ensuring safe and scientifically sound disposal. For recyclable waste, the Company engages 
with authorised waste recyclers, vendors, and agencies validated for regulatory compliance to ensure responsible recycling and 
disposal.
 Strategy to Reduce Hazardous and Toxic Chemical Usage:
  The Company is committed to reducing direct use of and exposure to hazardous and toxic chemicals in its products and processes 
through the following approaches:
 Process Automation:
  Automation has been introduced in relevant processes to minimise direct human exposure to hazardous materials, enhancing 
both worker safety and operational efficiency. 
 Material Substitution:
 Efforts to substitute hazardous chemicals with safer alternatives in manufacturing processes.
  Inventory Optimisation:
 Practices to optimise chemical inventory and reduce unnecessary procurement and usage of hazardous substances.
  All plants operate in full compliance with applicable operating permits and hazardous waste authorisations issued by the relevant 
regulatory authorities.

  The Company has established a Business Continuity and Disaster Management Plan to ensure operational resilience and 
employee safety during unforeseen events. Key measures in place include comprehensive risk assessments, emergency

  Physical safeguards across facilities include lightning arresters, a centralised fire alarm monitoring system, passive fire protection

by the EHS and HR teams.

PRINCIPLE 9
Businesses should engage with and provide value to their consumers in a responsible manner
1. Describe the mechanisms in place to receive and respond to consumer complaints and feedback.
  The Company has a defined process for receiving, investigating, and responding to complaints and feedback related to product 
quality from customers, distributors, and other stakeholders.
  Receipt of Complaints: Complaints and feedback can be submitted through the Company’s website via the ‘Contact Us’ section, 
which includes a dedicated ‘Product Complaint/Feedback’ form for registering relevant details.
  Investigation and Resolution: All complaints are investigated within 30 days of receipt. Upon completion of the investigation, 
appropriate corrective and preventive actions are identified and implemented to address the root cause and prevent recurrence.
  Response and Closure: Following investigation, a Complaint Reply Form is sent to the complainant detailing the findings and 
actions taken. The complainant is given 15 working days to provide any further comments or feedback. If no response is received 
within this period, the complaint is formally closed.
 Complaints are tracked centrally and reviewed periodically to identify recurring issues and drive systemic quality improvements.

To the Board of Directors of Amber Enterprises India Limited
1.  We have undertaken to perform a limited assurance engagement, for Amber Enterprises India Limited (“the Company”) 
vide Engagement Letter dated May 14, 2026 in respect of the agreed Sustainability Information listed in the “the “Identified 
Sustainability Information” paragraph below in accordance with the criteria stated in the “Criteria” paragraph below. The 
identified Sustainability information is included in the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (“BRSR”) of the company 
for the year ended March 31, 2026 pursuant to the requirement of Regulation 34(2)(f) of the Securities and Exchange Board of 
India’s (“SEBI”) (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (as amended) (the “LODR Regulations”). 
This engagement was conducted by a multidisciplinary team including assurance practitioners and specialists.
Identified Sustainability Information
2.  The Identified Sustainability Information for the year ended March 31, 2026 is BRSR Core (sub-set of BRSR), the attributes of 
which are summarised in Appendix 1 to this report. The Reporting Boundary for BRSR is on Consolidated basis as disclosed 
under Question No. 13 of Section A: General Disclosure of the BRSR.
3.  Our limited assurance engagement was with respect to the year ended March 31, 2026 information only and we have not 
performed any procedures with respect to earlier periods or any other elements included in the BRSR (i.e. non- BRSR Core 
attributes) and, therefore, do not express any conclusion thereon.
Criteria
4. The criteria used by the company to prepare the Identified Sustainability Information is summarized below:
 i.  Regulation 34(2)(f) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (the “SEBI”) (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements), Regulations, 2015 as amended;
 ii.  Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting Requirements for listed entities per Master Circular No. 
HO/49/14/14(7)2025-CFD-POD2/I/3762/2026 dated January 30, 2026.
Management’s Responsibility
5.  The Company’s management is responsible for selecting or establishing suitable criteria for preparing the Identified Sustainability 
Information including the reporting boundary of BRSR, taking into account applicable laws and regulations including the 
SEBI circular, related to reporting on the Identified Sustainability Information, identification of key aspects, engagement with 
stakeholders, content, preparation and presentation of the Identified Sustainability Information in accordance with the Criteria. 
This responsibility includes design, implementation and maintenance of internal controls relevant to the preparation of the 
BRSR and measurement of Identified Sustainability Information, which is free from material misstatement, whether due to 
fraud or error. The Management and the Board of Directors of the Company are also responsible for overseeing the Company’s 
compliance with the requirements of LODR Regulations and the SEBI Circular in relation to the BRSR.
Inherent limitations
6.  The absence of a significant body of established practice on which to draw to evaluate and measure non-financial indicators 
allows for different, but acceptable, measures and measurement techniques and can affect comparability between entities.
7.  Measurement of certain amounts and BRSR Core attributes, some of which are estimates, is subject to inherent measurement 
uncertainty, for example, GHG emissions, water footprint, energy footprint, embracing circularity (waste management). Obtaining 
sufficient appropriate evidence to support our conclusion does not reduce the uncertainty in the amounts and attributes.
Our Independence and Quality Control
8.  We have maintained our independence and confirm that we have met the requirements of the Code of Ethics issued by the 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and the SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CFD-SEC-2/P/CIR/2023/122 dated July 12, 
2023, and its clarifications thereto and have the required competencies and experience to conduct this assurance engagement.Annexure - G

Our Responsibility
10.  Our responsibility is to express a limited assurance conclusion on the Identified Sustainability Information listed in Appendix 1

11.  We conducted our limited assurance engagement in accordance with the Standard on Sustainability Assurance Engagements 
(SSAE) 3000, “Assurance Engagements on Sustainability Information” , issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board 
of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. This standard requires that we plan and perform our engagement to obtain 
limited assurance about whether the Identified Sustainability Information summarized in appendix 1 is free from material 
misstatement.
12.  A limited assurance engagement involves assessing the suitability in the circumstances of the Company’s use of the Criteria 
as the basis for the preparation of the Identified Sustainability Information, assessing the risks of material misstatement of 
the Identified Sustainability Information whether due to fraud or error, responding to the assessed risks as necessary in the 
circumstances, and evaluating the overall presentation of the Identified Sustainability Information.
13.  A limited assurance engagement is substantially less in scope than a reasonable assurance engagement in relation to both the 
risk assessment procedures, including an understanding of internal control, and the procedures performed in response to the 
assessed risks.
14.  The procedures we performed were based on our professional judgment and included inquiries, observation of processes 
performed, inspection of documents, evaluating the appropriateness of quantification methods and reporting policies, analytical 
procedures and agreeing or reconciling with underlying records.
15. Below is the informative summary of the procedures performed by us for obtaining limited assurance:
 • Obtained an understanding of the Identified Sustainability Information and related disclosures;
 •  Assessed the suitability of the criteria used by the entity in preparing the Identified Sustainability Information subject to 
limited assurance;
 •  Made inquiries of Company’s management, including those responsible for preparing the BRSR report, finance team, 
human resource team amongst others and those with the responsibility for managing the Company’s BRSR;
 •  Through inquiries, obtained an understanding of the control environment, processes and information systems relevant 
to the preparation of the information subject to limited assurance, but did not evaluate the design of particular control 
activities, obtain evidence about their implementation or test their operating effectiveness;
 •  Inspected, at each site visited, a limited number of samples as appropriate to check the accuracy of the data;
 •  Applied analytical procedures, as appropriate; and made inquiries of management to obtain explanations for any differences 
we identified;
 • Recalculated the information subject to limited assurance based on the criteria;
 •  Evaluated the overall presentation of the Identified Sustainability information subject to limited assurance to determine 
whether it is consistent with the criteria and in line with our overall knowledge of, and experience with, the entity’s 
operations.
 •  Where applicable, for the Identified Sustainability Information in the BRSR, we have relied on the information in the audited 
consolidated financial statements of the Company for the year ended March 31, 2026 and the underlying trial balance.
 •  Evaluated the reasonableness and appropriateness of significant estimates and judgements made by the management in 
the preparation of the Identified Sustainability Information.
 • Obtained representations from Company’s management.
  We also performed such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances.
  We believe that the evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our limited assurance 
conclusion.

A BRIEF STATEMENT ON COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON CODE

I.  COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON CODE OF GOVERNANCE
 Corporate governance is not merely a regulatory obligation  
it is a core component of your Company and a reflection 
of its commitment to ethical leadership, responsible 
management, and sustainable value creation.
 Our governance philosophy is deeply aligned with our 
Vision to be the FIRST CHOICE of Customers and our 
Mission is to become the No. 1 OEM/ODM and parts 
manufacturing company, while fostering growth and 
success for all stakeholders.
We believe that good governance is the foundation 
of trust, and trust is the cornerstone of long-term 
business success.
 Foundational Pillars of Governance
 Your Company’s governance model is built on three 
foundational pillars: Transparency, Accountability, and 
Security. These principles foster trust through clear 
communication, responsible leadership, and the protection 
of stakeholder interests. Our commitment to stakeholder 
satisfaction is evident in our consistent shareholder 
returns, strong credit ratings, industry recognitions, and 
sound governance practices.
Pillar Description
Transparency We ensure timely and accurate 
disclosure of policies and actions to all 
stakeholders.
Accountability We take responsibility for our actions 
and decisions, ensuring they align with 
our ethical standards.
Security We protect stakeholder interests 
through robust oversight, controls, and 
governance mechanisms.
 Key Attributes Guiding Our Approach
 Corporate governance at your Company is a reflection 
of our values, work culture, and strategic mindset. The 
following key attributes guide our approach:
• Transparency: We ensure timely and accurate 
disclosure of policies and actions to all stakeholders.
• Fairness: We operate with impartiality and integrity, 
striving to enhance shareholder value without 
conflicts of interest.
• Integrity: We uphold the accuracy and independent 
verification of our financial reporting.CORPORATE GOVERNANCE REPORTAnnexure - H
• Equity: We treat all stakeholders fairly and provide 
effective mechanisms for timely resolution of 
concerns.
• Accountability: We take responsibility for our actions 
and decisions, ensuring they align with our ethical 
standards.
 Core Values Shaping Our Governance
 Our governance philosophy is also shaped by our core 
values:
◆ Good Intentions – We act with honesty and purpose.
◆ Work Smart – We strive for efficiency and excellence.
◆ Drive Continuous Innovation – We challenge the 
status quo.
◆ Cultivate Happiness for All – We value the well-being 
of our employees, partners, and communities.
 Our Corporate Governance framework is dynamic and 
evolves with changing business environments, regulatory 
landscapes, and stakeholder expectations. It is designed 
to ensure that the Company remains agile, resilient, and 
responsible delivering sustainable value while upholding 
the trust placed in us by our stakeholders.
 Our governance philosophy is rooted in conscience, 
openness, fairness, and professionalism, forming a solid 
foundation of market confidence. These principles shape 
our vision and strategy, enabling us to adapt and thrive 
in a dynamic environment. We are dedicated to doing 
the “right things” in the “right way, ” ensuring financial 
strength, brand integrity, sustainability, and reliability for 
all shareholders.
II.  GOVERNANCE – FRAMEWORK, PRACTICES, POLICIES & 
STRUCTURE
 We believe that corporate governance is fundamentally 
about balancing the interests of all stakeholders  including 
shareholders, the Board of Directors, management team, 
employees, customers, suppliers, bankers, government 
authorities, and the broader community.
 Our governance framework is designed to facilitate 
effective, entrepreneurial and prudent management that 
can deliver sustainable business results over the long 
term. It ensures that the Company operates with integrity, 
transparency, and accountability, while remaining agile 
and responsive to the evolving needs of its stakeholders.
 Good corporate governance establishes a system of 
checks and balances, ensuring that the decision making 
powers vested in the executive management are exercised

 GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE  
 The Company has instituted a multi-tier internal governance structure that clearly defines the roles and responsibilities of each 
constituent within the system. This structure ensures effective oversight, strategic direction and operational accountability 
across all levels of the organisation.
 At the core of this framework:
ShareholdersThe ultimate owners of the Company, shareholders exercise their rights by appointing the Board of 
Directors, thereby entrusting them with the responsibility of governance and strategic leadership.
Board of DirectorsThe Board plays a pivotal role in overseeing the Company’s performance and ensuring alignment with 
its annual plan and long-term strategy. Its review encompasses financial results, the performance 
of subsidiaries, compliance status, liquidity position, investments, industrial relations, environmental 
approvals, and other regulatory matters.
The Board deliberates on matters relating to senior leadership, including appointments, remuneration, 
and succession planning. It provides periodic guidance on strategy, budgets, capital expenditure, 
investments, governance practices, shareholder returns, and ESG commitments, while taking into 
account prevailing economic conditions, regulatory changes, and industry developments.
To strengthen its perspective, the Board also engages with industry experts on critical issues whenever 
considered appropriate, thereby ensuring that its decisions remain well-informed and forward-looking.
Board CommitteesThe Board has constituted various Committees, each with a defined charter and scope, to discharge 
its responsibilities effectively. These include the Audit Committee, Nomination and Remuneration 
Committee, Corporate Social Responsibility Committee, Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee, 
Risk Management Committee, Business Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, and other  
sub-committees as required.
Executive 
ManagementLed by the Chief Executive Officer, Managing Director and Key Managerial Personnel, the executive 
management team is responsible for implementing the Board’s directives, managing day-to-day 
operations and ensuring compliance with policies and regulations.
Functional & 
Operational UnitsThese units operate under the guidance of executive management and are responsible for executing 
business strategies, maintaining operational efficiency and adhering to internal controls and governance 
policies.
Your Company has complied with the governance requirements of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, as amended from time to time (“SEBI LODR Regulations”) and hereby presents 
the Corporate Governance Report for the Financial Year ended 31st March 2026. This Report outlines the key aspects of the 
Company’s governance framework and governance practices which are consistent with the SEBI LODR Regulations and other 
rules and regulations.

  Directors and Officers Liability Insurance
 In compliance with the provisions of the Act and Regulation 25(10) of the SEBI LODR Regulations, the Company maintains 
a Directors and Officers Liability Insurance Policy (“D&O Policy”) for and on behalf of all its Directors, Officers, Employees 
and Independent Directors. The Policy provides comprehensive indemnity coverage against personal liability arising from 
actual or alleged acts of misrepresentation, misstatement, omission, defamation, negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, 
breach of warranty of authority, or any other wrongful act committed in the course of discharging their responsibilities and 
obligations to the Company.
 SELECTION AND APPOINTMENT OF NEW DIRECTORS
 The process for selection and appointment of Directors is overseen by the Nomination and Remuneration Committee 
(“NRC”) in accordance with the Act, the SEBI LODR Regulations, and the Company’s Diversity of Board of Directors Policy 
and Nomination and Remuneration Policy. The process follows a structured four stage framework:
1 Screening and Evaluation
The NRC undertakes a structured screening and evaluation of prospective candidates against Board approved 
criteria encompassing academic qualifications, domain expertise, professional experience, integrity, independence, 
and alignment with the Company’s long-term strategic objectives and governance philosophy.
2 Recommendation to the Board
Upon conclusion of the evaluation, the NRC presents its considered recommendation to the Board, accompanied 
by relevant assessments and a substantiated rationale for the proposed appointment.
3 Board Approval
The Board deliberates on the NRC’s recommendation and, upon being satisfied with the candidate’s suitability 
and credentials, accords its approval for the appointment, subject to the requisite shareholder approval.
4 Shareholders’ Approval
The proposed appointment is placed before the shareholders for approval at the General Meeting, in accordance 
with the Act and applicable regulatory requirements.
 Upon appointment, each Director receives a formal letter of appointment setting out the terms and conditions of 
engagement, fiduciary duties, key responsibilities, and the Board’s expectations. A specimen of the letter of appointment is 
disclosed on the Company’s website in accordance with applicable requirements.
 INDUCTION AND TRAINING OF BOARD MEMBERS
 The Company has a structured induction and familiarisation Programme for all Directors upon their appointment to the 
Board, in accordance with Regulation 25(7) of the SEBI LODR Regulations. Through focused orientation sessions conducted 
by Executive Directors and senior management, newly inducted Non-Executive and Independent Directors are familiarised 
with the Company’s culture, values, and strategic commitments.
 The induction Programme comprehensively covers the following areas:
• Business overview  - the Company’s operations, business model, product and service portfolio, and competitive 
positioning;
• Group architecture  - the organisational structure, subsidiary and associate companies, and key business relationships;
• Governance framework  - the Company’s constitutional documents, Board procedures, matters reserved for Board 
decision, and applicable statutory and regulatory requirements;
• Financial overview  - financial performance, capital structure, and key accounting policies;
• Risk management  - material enterprise risks and the Company’s risk management strategy and internal control 
framework.Annexure - H (Contd.)

 PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF THE BOARD
 Pursuant to Regulation 17(10) read with Schedule 
II Part D of the SEBI LODR Regulations, and the 
provisions of the Act read with Schedule IV thereto, 
the Board undertakes a formal and rigorous annual 
evaluation of the performance of the Board as 
a whole, its Committees, the Chairperson, and 
individual Directors including each Independent 
Director.
 The evaluation process is conducted through 
a structured questionnaire based assessment 
framework, covering the following dimensions:
• Board level evaluation: Adequacy of Board 
composition, quality and depth of deliberations, 
effectiveness of agenda management, strategic 
oversight, and adherence to governance 
standards.
• Committee-level evaluation: Fulfilment 
of the Committee’s terms of reference, 
quality of reporting to the Board, and overall 
effectiveness.
• Individual Director evaluation: Contributions 
to Board and Committee deliberations, 
attendance and preparedness, domain 
expertise, exercise of independent judgment, 
and engagement with management.
 The performance of each Independent Director 
is evaluated by the entire Board, excluding the 
Director being evaluated. The Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee reviews the evaluation 
outcomes and the results are shared with the full 
Board for consideration in informing Board level 
decisions on reappointments, succession planning, 
and governance improvements.
The Board is satisfied that the evaluation 
process provides a meaningful and objective 
assessment of individual and collective 
performance, and that its outcomes are actively 
used to enhance the effectiveness of the Board 
and its Committees. ROLE OF THE BOARD, BOARD PROCEDURE AND

 The Board of Directors functions as the ultimate

 CEO/CFO CERTIFICATION
 In accordance with Regulation 17(8) read with Schedule 
II Part B of the SEBI LODR Regulations, the Executive 
Chairman & Chief Executive Officer and Whole Time 
Director (“CEO”) and the Chief Financial Officer (“CFO”) of 
the Company furnish a certificate to the Board of Directors 
on an annual basis.
 The said certificate covers, inter alia, an affirmation that 
the financial statements and cash flow statement of 
the Company present a true and fair view of its state of 
affairs, and that to the best of their knowledge and belief, 
no transactions have been entered into by the Company 
which are fraudulent, illegal or in violation of the Company’s 
Code of Conduct. The certificate further confirms the 
establishment and maintenance of adequate internal 
controls for financial reporting, and the reporting of any 
significant deficiencies or material weaknesses therein to 
the Statutory Auditors and the Audit Committee.
 Separately, in compliance with Regulation 33(2)(a) of the 
SEBI LODR Regulations, the CEO and CFO are required to 
certify to the Board of Directors, while placing the quarterly 
financial results before it and prior to their submission 
to the Stock Exchanges, that the financial results do not 
contain any false or misleading statement or figures 
and do not omit any material fact which may render the 
statements or figures contained therein misleading.
 For the Financial Year 2025–26, the certificate pursuant 
to Regulation 17(8), duly signed by the CEO and the CFO, 
was placed before the Board at its meeting held on 15th 
May 2026. 
 The said certificate is annexed to this Report and forms 
an integral part of the Company’s commitment to sound 
financial governance and regulatory compliance.
 BOARD EVALUATION
 The Board evaluation is an integral part of the Company’s 
commitment to good corporate governance. An annual 
evaluation of the Board, its Committees, the Chairman, 
and individual Directors is carried out in accordance with 
the provisions of the Act and the SEBI LODR Regulations. This process reinforces transparency, accountability, and 
effectiveness, while enabling the Board to identify areas 
for improvement and align governance practices with best 
standards.
 The Nomination and Remuneration Committee (“NRC”) 
has formulated the criteria for evaluation of the 
performance of Directors, Key Managerial Personnel, 
Senior Management Personnel, the Board as a whole and 
its Committees, in accordance with the requirements of 
Section 178 of the Act and Schedule II Part D of the SEBI 
LODR Regulations. The annual performance evaluation 
was carried out during Financial Year 2025–26 based on 
the said criteria.
 Performance Evaluation Process
 Step 1: Evaluation of Board Committees
•	 Self-evaluation forms were circulated to the 
members of the respective Board Committees along 
with the agenda papers for their meetings.
•	 Each Committee undertook a self-assessment of its 
performance and effectiveness.
•	 The Chairpersons of the respective Committees 
submitted summary evaluation reports to the Board.
•	 The outcome of the Committee evaluations was 
placed before the Board for its review and noting.
 Step 2: Evaluation of Individual Directors and the Board
•	 Based on the approved evaluation framework, the 
performance of individual Directors and the Board as 
a whole was evaluated.
•	 The performance evaluation of Independent 
Directors, Non-Independent Directors and Board 
Committees was carried out by the Board, excluding 
the Director being evaluated.
 Step 3: Separate Meeting of Independent Directors
•	 The Independent Directors, at their separate 
meeting, evaluated: 
o the performance of Non-Independent 
Directors;
o the performance of the Board as a whole; and
o the performance of the Executive Chairman & 
Chief Executive Officer and Whole Time Director 
and Managing Director.
•	 While undertaking the evaluation, the Independent 
Directors considered the views of the Executive and 
Non-Executive Directors.Annexure - H (Contd.)

=== page 271 ===
 Step 4: Consolidation and Review of Evaluation Results
•	 The inputs received from the Board, individual 
Directors and Board Committees were consolidated 
and presented to the Board.
•	 Mr. Jasbir Singh, Chairperson of the Board, reviewed 
the overall evaluation outcomes and the consolidated 
evaluation reports.
 Step 5: Board’s Conclusion
•	 The consolidated evaluation reports were placed 
before the Board for its consideration.
•	 Based on the evaluation exercise, the Board noted its 
satisfaction with the performance and effectiveness 
of the Board, its committees and individual Directors.
•	 The Directors also expressed satisfaction that 
the evaluation process was conducted in a fair, 
transparent and effective manner.
 The Directors expressed their satisfaction with the overall 
evaluation process, affirming that it was conducted in a 
fair, transparent, and effective manner.

 COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD
 In line with sound corporate governance practices, the Board of Directors has constituted several Committees to facilitate 
focused deliberation on specific functional areas. Each Committee operates within clearly defined terms of reference approved 
by the Board and exercises delegated authority in its respective domain. The Board remains ultimately responsible for the 
actions of its Committees. Chairpersons of each Committee brief the Board at its meetings, and the minutes of all Committee 
meetings are placed before the Board for review and noting.
A.  Audit Committee
 The Audit Committee has been constituted in accordance with Section 177 of the Act and Regulation 18 read with Part C 
of Schedule II of the SEBI LODR Regulations.
 The primary objective of the Audit Committee is to provide oversight of the Company’s financial reporting process, the 
integrity of its financial statements, the adequacy and reliability of internal control systems, compliance with legal and 
regulatory requirements, and the performance of statutory and internal auditors. It monitors the financial reporting process 
to ensure accurate, timely and transparent disclosures.

 Formal Annual Evaluation
 The NRC plays a pivotal role in strengthening the 
Board’s governance framework through structured 
evaluation and succession planning.
 Performance Evaluation
 Pursuant to Section 134(3)(p) of the Act and 
Schedule II Part D of SEBI LODR Regulations, the 
NRC formulates the evaluation framework and 
criteria, and recommends these to the Board. The 
Board conducts the formal annual evaluation of its 
own performance, individual Directors (including 
Independent Directors), and each Board Committee, 
using structured questionnaires developed by the 
NRC. 
 The NRC also undertakes a self-evaluation of its own 
effectiveness annually.
 The evaluation questionnaires cover the following 
key dimensions:
•	 Composition, diversity and skills mix of the 
Board and Committees;
•	 Board culture, dynamics and effectiveness of 
deliberations;
•	 Execution of fiduciary duties and governance 
responsibilities; and
•	 Quality of strategic oversight and decisio n 
making.
 These questionnaires are aligned with the SEBI 
Guidance Note on Board Evaluation (Circular dated 
5th January 2017, notified on 31st July 2018). For 
Independent Directors, evaluation specifically 
considers attendance, relevant skills and experience, 
quality of participation, and knowledge of the 
Company’s business and industry.

 The NRC, in collaboration with the Human Resources 
function, maintains a structured leadership 
succession framework covering Director, Senior 
Management and other critical roles. Senior leaders Annexure - H (Contd.)

Association of the Company, not less than two-thirds

every AGM, one-third of such Directors are liable to retire 
by rotation or, if their number is not three or a multiple of 
three, the number nearest to one-third shall retire from 
office and, being eligible, may offer themselves for re-
appointment.
 The director(s) to retire at each AGM shall be those who 
have been longest in office since their last appointment 
or re-appointment, and as between persons who became

 Remuneration Philosophy and Governance
 The remuneration of Directors and Key Managerial 
Personnel (“KMPs”) is determined by the Board of 
Directors, based on the recommendations of the 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee (“NRC”). In 
formulating its recommendations, the NRC considers 
several factors, including:
•	 The financial position and scale of operations of the 
Company;
•	 Industry benchmarks and compensation structures 
of comparable peer companies;
•	 The qualifications, experience, competencies and 
past performance of the individual;
•	 The long-term strategic interests and value creation 
objectives of the Company; and
•	 Applicable regulatory requirements, including the 
provisions of Section 197 of the Act.
 The Company confirms that the remuneration paid to its 
Whole Time Directors and other managerial personnel 
during Financial Year 2025-26 is within the overall limits 
prescribed under Section 197 of the Act, as approved by 
the members of the Company.

 RISK MANAGEMENT
 Risk management is a structured and proactive approach 
to managing uncertainty and ensuring business resilience. 
The Company recognises that risks whether arising from 
strategic, operational, financial, compliance or external 
factors must be systematically identified, assessed, 
monitored and mitigated to protect stakeholder value 
and ensure the continuity of business operations.
 Governance Framework
 Pursuant to Regulation 17(9) and Regulation 21 of the 
SEBI LODR Regulations, the Board of Directors has 
adopted a formal Risk Management Policy and constituted 
a Risk Management Committee (“RMC”) to oversee and 
monitor the risk management framework. The details of 
the RMC including its composition, terms of reference 
and meetings are set out in the Committees of the Board 
section of this Report.
 The risk management governance structure operates 
across three levels:
•	 The Board of Directors responsible for framing, 
approving and monitoring the overall Risk 
Management Policy and framework, in compliance Annexure - H (Contd.)
with Regulation 17(9) of SEBI LODR Regulations. The 
Board reviews the adequacy and effectiveness of the 
risk management framework periodically.
•	 The RMC reviews and approves the Risk Management 
Policy at least once in a year, as required under 
Regulation 21(4) of SEBI LODR Regulations; reviews 
key risks and the adequacy of mitigation measures; 
and reports findings to the Board.
•	 The Management is responsible for day-to-
day identification, assessment, monitoring and 
mitigation of risks across all operational and strategic 
units, with findings reported to the RMC.
 Risk Management Framework
 The Company has adopted an enterprise-wide 
risk management framework that integrates risk 
considerations into strategic planning, annual business 
planning cycles and periodic management reviews. All 
operational and strategic business units are aligned with 
the Company’s Risk Management Policy and Guidelines, 
ensuring that risk awareness and responsiveness are 
embedded into the Company’s decision-making culture 
and multi-business, multi-site operations.
 The framework is designed to be dynamic evolving in 
response to changes in the business environment and 
is oriented towards maintaining an optimal risk-reward 
balance that enhances long-term shareholder value. 
Adequate systems and skilled personnel are deployed 
across the enterprise for risk identification, assessment, 
monitoring and mitigation.
 Key Risks and Mitigation Measures
 The Company has identified the principal risk categories. 
Key risks within each category, along with the mitigation 
measures adopted, are set out in the respective sections 
of the Annual Report.
 The Risk Management Policy of the Company, as reviewed 
and approved by the RMC and the Board during Financial Year  
2025-26, provides the overarching framework for 
enterprise risk management. The Policy is periodically 
reviewed and updated to remain responsive to the 
evolving risk landscape.

 SEBI Complaint Redress System (“SCORES 2.0”)
 Investor complaints are processed in a centralised web-
based complaint redress system. The salient features of 
this system are: a centralised database of all complaints, 
online upload of Action Taken Reports by the concerned 
company, and online viewing by investors of the actions 
taken on their complaint and its current status.
 A new version of the SEBI Complaint Redress System, 
namely SCORES 2.0, was launched with effect from  
1st April 2024. The key steps under this mechanism for 
complaint redressal are as follows:
(1)  All listed companies that receive a complaint from 
investors through SCORES 2.0 shall resolve the 
complaint within 21 calendar days and submit 
an Action Taken Report (“ATR”) for the complaint 
through SCORES 2.0.
(2)  The ATR submitted by the listed company through 
SCORES 2.0 will be automatically routed to the 
complainant.
(3)  Upon receipt of the ATR from the listed company, if 
the complainant is not satisfied, the complaint may 
be escalated for a first review to the Stock Exchange; 
such escalated complaints will be addressed by the 
Exchange within Ten (10) calendar days.
(4)  Subsequent to the first review by the Exchange, if 
the investor remains dissatisfied with the resolution, 
the complaint may be escalated for a second review 
to SEBI.
(5)  At any stage, in the event of non-adherence to the 
prescribed timelines by the listed company or the 
Exchange, as the case may be, the complaint will be 
automatically escalated to the next level.
(6)  At any stage, the investor has the option to refer the 
complaint to the Online Dispute Resolution (“ODR”) 
mechanism. Once a complaint has been referred to 
ODR, it shall be treated as disposed of in SCORES 2.0.

demat and physical folio holders, accounts shall not 
be frozen, nor payments withheld solely on account 
of missing nomination details, and debit transactions 
in demat accounts are similarly protected from such 
restrictions.
 For demat account holders, nomination is mandatory 
for new accounts, unless the account is held jointly. For 
existing demat accounts, nomination remains optional; 
however, SEBI strongly encourages nominations to 
facilitate smooth succession and prevent unclaimed 
assets.
 As part of its ongoing compliance and investor awareness 
efforts, the Company has: (a) sent targeted e-mail alerts 
to all shareholders in physical form identifying missing 
compliance information; (b) ensured that depositories, 
depository participants, asset management companies 
and RTAs issue pop-up alerts, e-mail and SMS reminders 
to shareholders who have not updated their nomination 
details; and (c) processed KYC and nomination details upon 
receipt, enabling immediate resumption of payments and 
shareholder services post compliance.

x) Disclosure of commodity price risk or foreign 
exchange risk and hedging activities
 The Company has an approved Risk Management 
Policy providing a framework for identification, 
assessment and mitigation of various business and 
financial risks, including commodity price and foreign 
exchange risks. The Board of Directors has overall 
responsibility for the Company’s risk management 
framework, while the Risk Management Committee 
oversees the hedging plan/policy and monitors 
hedging activities.
 Exposure to Commodity and Commodity Risks 
during the Financial Year
 During the Financial Year 2025-26, the Company 
was exposed to fluctuations in the prices of key 
raw materials used in its manufacturing operations, 
including copper, aluminium, steel and other metals. 
The Company actively monitored commodity price 
movements and managed such risks through 
procurement planning, cost optimisation and, 
wherever feasible, appropriate price pass-through 
mechanisms.
a.  Total exposure of the Company to 
commodities in INR:
	 The Company did not have any direct 
commodity trading exposure. Its commodity 
exposure primarily arose from the procurement

of raw materials used in its manufacturing 
operations. Based on the Company’s

b.  Exposure of the Company to various

	 The Company’s principal commodity price

 Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging Activities
 The Company was exposed to foreign exchange

Compliance Certificate from Practicing Company Secretary Regarding Compliance of Conditions of Corporate Governance under 
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, as amended (“SEBI LODR Regulations”)
1.  Background 
 I have been approached by Amber Enterprises India Limited (“the Company”) to examine the compliance with the conditions of 
Corporate Governance by the Company, as stipulated in the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015 (the “SEBI LODR Regulations”), as amended from time to time, for the Financial Year ended 31st March 2026. 
2.  Management’s Responsibility
 The compliance of conditions of Corporate Governance stipulated in the SEBI LODR Regulations is the responsibility of the 
Management. The Management shall devise adequate systems, internal controls and processes to monitor and ensure the 
same.
3.  My Responsibility
 My responsibility is limited to conducting an examination of the systems, internal controls and processes adopted by the 
Company and implementation thereof to monitor and ensure compliance with the conditions of Corporate Governance and 
report thereon.
4.  Methodology
4.1.  In order to conduct my examination, I was provided with the relevant documents and information including explanations, 
wherever required.
4.2.  My examination was conducted in a manner which provided me with a reasonable basis for evaluating the systems, internal 
controls and processes adopted by the Company to monitor and ensure compliance with the conditions of Corporate 
Governance and to issue this certificate thereon.

(A) Conservation of Energy :
Energy Conservation and Environmental Sustainability
Energy conservation remains a core focus at your Company manufacturing facilities. Through continuous improvement 
initiatives, we optimise fuel, power, and water usage by benchmarking performance, setting consumption baselines, and 
identifying efficiency losses.
Environmental sustainability is deeply embedded in Company’s Environmental Policy. As a responsible manufacturer, energy 
conservation is integral to our operations. We strive to balance industrial growth with environmental care, ensuring our 
products, packaging, and operations remain safe for all stakeholders of the Company and the environment. Our focus remains 
on ecofriendly technologies and process enhancements.
Your Company employees are regularly trained in energy saving practices. 
(i) Steps taken or impact on 
conservation of energyCommitment to Environmental Sustainability:
Your Company recognises its responsibility in conserving natural resources and promoting 
sustainability. As part of our overarching sustainability strategy, the environmental component is 
focused on minimising the ecological footprint of our operations and supporting the preservation 
of the natural environment.
Some of the key energy and resource efficiency initiatives undertaken during the Financial Year 
2025 – 26 are as under :
  Unit: Dehradun – DDN-5
The unit implemented a timer-based automated control system in the cooler supply line to 
eliminate unnecessary energy consumption during non-productive periods. Previously, eight 
industrial coolers each with a capacity of 3 kW and an aggregate installed capacity of 24 kW   
operated continuously throughout each shift, including during tea breaks, lunch intervals, and 
post-shift hours. The automated timer system now switches off the coolers during these non-
working intervals without requiring manual intervention, eliminating approximately one hour 
of unnecessary operation per shift. This initiative has resulted in estimated energy savings 
of approximately 624 kW per month, with a commensurate reduction in electricity costs and 
improvement in overall energy efficiency.
  Unit: Dehradun – DDN-6 / DDN-4
Two energy conservation measures were undertaken at the DDN-6 unit. The first involved a 
systematic reduction in lighting energy consumption through replacement of existing 150W auto-
cut lights with energy efficient 120W units, reducing power consumption per luminaire by 20W 
while maintaining prescribed illumination standards and contributing to lower electricity costs and 
reduced carbon emissions.
At Unit DDN-4, 100W LED fixtures were replaced with 76W LED lights across three production 
lines (six luminaires in total), achieving a 24% reduction in power consumption per fitting while 
sustaining adequate illumination. The project was completed at a capital expenditure of `12,000 
and is operational without interruption.
  Unit: Amber Rudrapur
The Amber Rudrapur unit undertook five distinct energy conservation initiatives during the Financial 
Year 2025-26.
First, a single Mould Temperature Controller (MTC) was deployed to simultaneously manage two 
1,000-tonne injection moulding machines (60°C ± 2°C), extended further so two MTCs now 
govern four machines through interlocking. Implemented without capital expenditure, this yields 
estimated annual savings of approximately `17 Lakh in energy and electrical costs.

Annexure - I (Contd.)
Second, a timer-controlled relay automated the Pre-Cure Oven (PCO) startup, replacing manual 
activation 90 minutes before shift start with a precise 45-minute automated interval. This 
generated estimated annual LPG savings of approximately `6,87,960 with no capital expenditure.
Third, a temperature sensor ( `540) was installed to trigger industrial cooling fans only when 
ambient temperature exceeds 25 °C, reducing daily electricity consumption from 652 to 541 units 
during winter and yielding monthly savings of approximately `26,000.
Fourth, a unified emergency stop button was installed to simultaneously halt all motors across 
three press shop lines during tool changeovers, saving 40 electrical units per day at an investment 
of `6,500.
Fifth, production of Control Cover and PCB components previously requiring four dedicated 
machines was restructured to use a single machine per component type, eliminating electricity 
consumption of two continuously operating machines with no capital expenditure.
  Unit: Sricity-I
Part-detection sensors with timer controls were installed to interlock oven heater blowers with 
coil presence across three paint-drying ovens (32 heaters) in HE and IDU lines. For IDU ovens, low 
power mode activates after 10 minutes of coil absence and full shutdown after 20 minutes; HE 
ovens shut down after 10 minutes. This in-house initiative delivers energy savings of 19,584 KWA 
per day across both shops.
Magnetic resonators were also installed along LPG supply pipelines to prevent molecular settling 
and enable complete combustion. An investment of `9.6 Lakh has achieved LPG savings of 5–6% 
per month.
  Unit: Jhajjar-I
The Cooling Tower Fan Motor, previously at full load (50 Hz, star-delta), was upgraded with a VFD 
reducing load to 80% in summer (40 Hz) and 60% in winter (30 Hz), leveraging the cubic fan speed-
power relationship for significant electricity savings. Investment: `1.0 Lakh.
Similarly, the Air Washer Blower Motor in the moulding area was upgraded with a VFD to operate 
at 40 Hz, achieving approximately 20% electricity savings. Investment: `1.0 Lakh.
  Unit: Jhajjar-II
Motion sensing lighting technology was deployed across plant areas, reducing power consumption 
from 100W to 13W per fixture when no movement is detected. This has delivered substantial 
electricity savings, with greater impact during off-season and partial-operation periods.
Effective March 2026, the unit transitioned from LPG to Piped Natural Gas (PNG) for its Paint Shop 
ovens, Assembly line brazing sections, Copper Shop brazing sections, and Heat Exchanger Shop 
ovens and brazing sections. PNG offers higher combustion efficiency, reduced handling losses, 
and consistent supply pressure compared to LPG, resulting in lower specific fuel consumption and 
reduced carbon emissions across these operations.
  Unit: Kanchipuram
The Kanchipuram unit implemented a comprehensive range of energy conservation measures 
spanning compressor management, electrical efficiency, lighting, process optimisation, and fuel 
consumption reduction.
In compressor operations, three compressors were interconnected to enable optimised, 
need based operation, eliminating the continuous running of all units irrespective of demand. 
Additionally, a dedicated 45 kW air compressor was installed exclusively for the Injection Moulding 
shop to provide a stable and right-sized compressed air supply, avoiding energy losses associated 
with shared systems operating at sub-optimal loads.

An Automatic Power Factor Correction (APFC) system was installed in the Press Shop to 
continuously monitor and stabilise the power factor within the range of 0.7 to 0.9. This improvement

and enhances overall electrical efficiency of the unit.
Dual Lux / smart lighting was installed in the store area, enabling dynamic control of illumination

50% reduction in lighting energy consumption in the relevant areas.
An automatic power cut-off system was implemented across Injection Moulding and Press 
Shop machines, configured to disconnect power supply after three minutes of machine idling. 
This eliminates standby energy losses during break periods, shift changeovers, and unplanned 
stoppages, materially reducing idle power consumption across the shop floor.
Magnetic resonators were installed on the LPG supply line in the Paint Shop and Heat Exchanger 
line to improve combustion efficiency by maintaining continuous molecular movement in the 
supply pipes. This initiative has reduced LPG consumption at the unit by approximately 12%.
The coating oven was converted from an electric-powered to an LPG-fired oven, reducing overall 
energy consumption for the coating process. The conversion also enhanced process throughput, 
with Units Per Hour (UPH) improving from 120 to 220, resulting in both energy and productivity 
gains.
  Unit: Ecotech-1

air systems, fuel consumption, idle power, and lighting.
An Intelligent Flow Control (IFC) system was implemented in the compressor network to 
dynamically regulate compressed air supply in line with actual demand, reducing compressor 
utilisation and associated operating costs by approximately 18%. The system is complemented 
by a Godrej Air Monitoring System for real-time tracking of compressed air consumption, and 
energy-efficient nozzles were fitted on air guns to reduce localised air wastage.
Magnetic resonators were installed in the Paint Shop PNG supply line, achieving a reduction in 
PNG consumption of approximately 6% per month through improved combustion efficiency.
An automatic power cut-off system was implemented at Press Shop machines, set to disconnect 
power supply after three minutes of idling, eliminating standby energy losses during non-
productive intervals.
Motion sensors were installed on Manufacturing Office lights to automatically deactivate lighting 
in unoccupied areas. Additionally, ES25 energy-saving devices were installed, achieving a 17% 
reduction in power consumption for lighting loads across the applicable areas.
  Unit: Ranjangaon
The Ranjangaon unit installed magnetic resonators in the Paint Shop PNG supply pipeline to 
prevent gas molecular settling and improve combustion completeness. This initiative has achieved 
a significant reduction of approximately 33% in PNG consumption per month, representing one of 
the highest fuel efficiency gains recorded across the Company’s units through this technology.
  Unit: Rajpura
The Rajpura unit implemented four energy conservation initiatives during the Financial Year  
2025–26.
Magnetic resonators were installed on the Paint Shop PNG supply pipeline, resulting in a reduction 
of approximately 6% in PNG consumption through enhanced combustion efficiency.
The diesel-fired Heat Exchanger was converted to PNG fuel, enabling exhaust gas recirculation and 
substantially reducing CO₂ emissions from this operation while improving fuel utilisation efficiency.

Press machine lighting was upgraded from 15W to 9W fixtures, reducing lighting energy 
consumption in the press shop area by 40% per fitting while maintaining adequate illumination 
levels.
A process optimisation was carried out in the Seam Welding water circulation system, where three 
separate 1-inch diameter water lines, each with an individual 3 HP motor (totalling 9 HP), were 
replaced with a single 3-inch diameter pipeline served by a single 5 HP motor. This consolidation 
eliminated redundant motor capacity, reducing total installed motor power from 9 HP to 5 HP and 
delivering a proportionate reduction in energy consumption for water circulation.
  Unit: SUPA
Effective March 2026, the SUPA unit transitioned from LPG to Piped Natural Gas (PNG) for its 
Paint Shop ovens, Assembly line brazing sections, and Heat Exchanger Shop ovens and brazing

carbon intensity, and continuous piped supply to reduce specific fuel consumption and operational 
emissions across the unit’s thermal processes.
  Unit: Sricity-II
The Sricity-II unit operates on Piped Natural Gas (PNG) as the primary fuel source for its Paint 
Shop ovens, Assembly line brazing sections, Copper Shop brazing sections, and Heat Exchanger 
Shop ovens and brazing sections. The adoption of PNG across all thermal processes ensures 
efficient combustion, eliminates LPG handling and storage risks, and contributes to reduced 
carbon emissions compared to conventional LPG based operations.
  Unit: R&D Centre
The R&D Centre implemented four energy conservation measures focused on power 
management, cooling efficiency, lighting upgrades, and fuel optimisation for laboratory 
operations.
A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) system was introduced in Psychometric Laboratory 
No. 7 to prevent power interruptions arising from grid failures. Beyond ensuring continuity 
of laboratory operations, the installation supports energy efficiency through balanced load 
management, reducing the energy losses and voltage fluctuations typically associated with grid 
instability.
Fresh Air Coolers in the R&D Offices are now controlled through timer-based systems configured 
to switch on and off at defined intervals, replacing continuous operation. This intervention 
eliminates unnecessary cooling energy consumption during unoccupied or low-activity periods, 
resulting in significant energy savings in the office cooling load.
Halogen light fixtures across the facility have been replaced with LED luminaires, significantly 
reducing lighting power consumption. LED technology consumes substantially less energy than 
halogen equivalents for the same lumen output, delivering both energy and maintenance cost 
savings.
The three 500 KVA diesel generator sets serving the laboratory facility have been synchronised 
and reconfigured to operate individually in sequence based on actual running load, rather than 
operating all units simultaneously. This load matched operation approach eliminates fuel wastage 
from running oversized generation capacity at low load factors, materially reducing diesel 
consumption across laboratory operations.
The number of motion sensors deployed across the facility was expanded from 45 to 55 units, 
extending automated lighting control to additional areas. The increased sensor coverage 
ensures that lights are activated only when areas are occupied, reducing unnecessary lighting 
usage and delivering significant energy and cost savings incrementally over the previous sensor 
deployment.Annexure - I (Contd.)
